elements.quote: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine the associations between food insecurity and key metabolic risk factors on the causal pathway to diet-sensitive NCDs and estimate the prevalence of key metabolic risk factors among the food-insecure patients in sub-Saharan Africa.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review and meta-analysis.

elements.quote: This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine the associations between food insecurity and key metabolic risk factors on the causal pathway to diet-sensitive NCDs and estimate the prevalence of key metabolic risk factors among the food-insecure patients in sub-Saharan Africa.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit statement of the main objective/review question.
The abstract does not specify the main inclusion and exclusion criteria (e.g., study design, population, time frame).

elements.quote: The following databases were searched for relevant literature: PubMed, EBSCOhost (CINAHL with full text, Health Source - Nursing, MedLine).
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the information sources used but fails to report when each source was last searched.

elements.quote: The Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) - Version 2018 was used to appraise included studies critically.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method used to assess risk of bias (MMAT).

elements.quote: Metaanalysis was performed with DerSimonian-Laird's random-effect model at 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the methods used to synthesize the results (meta-analysis with random-effects model).

elements.quote: 22 cross-sectional studies were eligible for inclusion, presenting data from 26,609 (46.8% males) food-insecure participants
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and participants.

elements.quote: The meta-analysis showed a significantly high pooled prevalence estimate of key metabolic risk factors among food-insecure participants at 41.8% (95% CI: 33.2% to 50.8%, I 2 = 99.5% p -value < 0.00) derived from 19 studies. The most prevalent type of metabolic risk factors was dyslipidaemia 27.6% (95% CI: 6.5% to 54.9%), hypertension 24.7% (95% CI: 15.6% to 35.1%), and overweight 15.8% (95% CI: 10.6% to 21.7%).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes, including the number of studies and participants (implied by the total) and summary estimates.

elements.quote: The meta-analysis showed a significantly high pooled prevalence estimate of key metabolic risk factors among food-insecure participants at 41.8% (95% CI: 33.2% to 50.8%, I 2 = 99.5% p -value < 0.00) derived from 19 studies.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the summary estimate and confidence interval for the meta-analysis.

The abstract does not explicitly indicate the direction of effect and which group is favored when comparing groups (e.g., male vs female prevalence differences are mentioned, but not in a comparative effect direction format).
The abstract does not summarize important limitations of the included evidence.

elements.quote: In this systematic review and meta-analysis, exposure to food insecurity was adversely associated with a wide spectrum of key metabolic risk factors, such as obesity, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, underweight, and overweight. These findings highlight the need to address food insecurity as an integral part of diet-sensitive NCDs prevention programmes.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and their implications.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.

elements.quote: PROSPERO registration number: PROSPERO 2019 CRD42019136638.
elements.reason: The abstract provides the register name (PROSPERO) and registration number.

elements.quote: While there are progressively better estimates of the prevalence of metabolic risk factors and proximate drivers of this prevalence in high-income countries; reliable data on the trend and patterns of key metabolic risk factors among the food insecure population in resource-limited settings, such as sub-Saharan African countries still lag far behind
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state of knowledge (better estimates in high-income countries) and the important uncertainty/gap (lack of reliable data in sub-Saharan Africa).

elements.quote: The primary objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to use accumulated evidence published between January 2015 and June 2019, to determine the associations between food insecurity and key metabolic risk factors for diet-sensitive NCDs. After analysing the accumulated evidence of associations, and identifying the spectrum of metabolic risk factors associated with food insecurity, the secondary outcome was the prevalence estimates of these metabolic risk factors among the food insecure participants in sub-Saharan Africa.
elements.reason: The authors explain the objectives of the review, which establishes the need for conducting the review to address the identified knowledge gap.

elements.quote: Previous systematic reviews and several cross-sectional studies have contributed to the evidence that food insecurity is associated with metabolic risk factors on the causal pathway to diet-sensitive NCDs. In the current review, the results of both analyses show imperative similarities, consistent with and expands the results of earlier reports.
elements.reason: The authors acknowledge previous systematic reviews (e.g., Arenas et al., Beltran et al.) and explain how their current review expands upon or relates to these existing findings.
This is a systematic review of observational studies (cross-sectional) assessing associations and prevalence, not a review of intervention effects.
This is not a review of complex interventions or delivery contexts; it is an epidemiological review of associations and prevalence.

elements.quote: The main research question: What are the associations between food insecurity and key metabolic risk factors for diet-sensitive NCDs in the sub-Saharan African population?
elements.reason: The review explicitly states its main research question using the PEO (Population, Exposure, and Outcomes) framework, which is a relevant question-formulation framework for this type of study.
This is not a review of intervention effects (it is an observational study review), so the requirement to state planned comparisons using PICO is not applicable.

elements.quote: Study design: Only original and quantitative study design that are peer-reviewed cross- sectional studies conducted in sub-Saharan Africa by trained personnel, in any publication language... Population: Studies conducted among sub-Saharan African populations Participants of any age group and sex that did not mix the age groups for analysis Any ethnicity, culture, or race... Exposure: Studies reporting a measure of food insecurity or food insufficiency as an inde- pendent variable... Outcomes: Studies reporting at least one of the key metabolic risk factors as a dependent variable
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies the study design (cross-sectional), setting (sub-Saharan Africa), and population characteristics (any age/sex) in Table 2. The PEO framework (Population, Exposure, Outcomes) is also described in the text and Table 1.

elements.quote: Time: Complete peer-reviewed original research studies, published between January 2015 and June 2019
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies the publication date range (January 2015 to June 2019) in Table 2. Language criteria are also specified as "any publication language" in Table 2.
The review does not report excluding studies based on whether outcomes were measured versus reported, so this conditional requirement does not apply.

elements.quote: The associations between food insecurity and metabolic risk outcomes were identified by coding the accumulated evidence on the associations into three strata, namely: [-] Adverse associations, [+] Non-significant associations, and [~] Inconclusive associations.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies how studies were grouped for synthesis (stratified into three categories: Adverse, Non-significant, and Inconclusive associations) and links these to the review objectives.

elements.quote: However, the year of publication was limited to between January 2015 and October 2019 to ensure that the evidence of associations is demonstrably rooted in the most recent and up-to-date scientific literature. This decision was chiefly because practitioners and decision-makers are somewhat interested and encouraged to make use of the most current evidence to inform policy debates
elements.reason: The manuscript provides a rationale for the restriction on the publication year (2015-2019) to ensure the evidence is current for policy debates.

elements.quote: The primary searches, both electronic and hand-searching, was performed simultaneously by the first author with the assistance of a professional university librarian from 15 May to 28 June 2019.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the date range for the primary searches (15 May to 28 June 2019).

elements.quote: Electronic searches -To identify relevant studies assessing the associations between food insecurity and metabolic risk factors, advanced search strategies were applied in the following electronic bibliographic databases (and ͹ Vol.:(0123456789) platforms): PubMed, EBSCOhost (CINAHL with full text, Health Source - Nursing, MedLine), Ovid (Journals@ Ovid Full Text), Web of Science (SCiELO Citation Index) and supplementary sources in Google Scholar platform.
elements.reason: The manuscript lists the bibliographic databases searched (PubMed, EBSCOhost, Ovid, Web of Science) and mentions Google Scholar.
No study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories were reported as searched.

elements.quote: supplementary sources in Google Scholar platform.
elements.reason: Google Scholar is identified as a supplementary source.

elements.quote: In addition, several subject specialists, medical professionals, and university librarian experts in the field were approached to identify additional relevant studies.
elements.reason: The manuscript notes that subject specialists, medical professionals, and university librarian experts were approached to identify studies.

elements.quote: In addition, several subject specialists, medical professionals, and university librarian experts in the field were approached to identify additional relevant studies.
elements.reason: The types of individuals contacted (subject specialists, medical professionals, university librarian experts) are described.

elements.quote: Hand-search -The electronic searches were further supplemented by hand-searching the bibliographies (reference lists) of all eligible studies for inclusion and the previously published systematic reviews of a relevant topic.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies that reference lists of eligible studies and previously published systematic reviews were hand-searched.
No formal backward or forward citation searching (e.g., using citation indices) is reported as a distinct search method, other than the general hand-searching of reference lists.
No specific journals or conference proceedings were consulted as a primary search method.

The manuscript states that details of the search strategies are in 'Supplementary Appendix No.1 - Table 1', but this supplementary material was not provided in the retrieved evidence. Therefore, the complete search strategy is not present.

elements.quote: However, the year of publication was limited to between January 2015 and October 2019 to ensure that the evidence of associations is demonstrably rooted in the most recent and up-to-date scientific literature.
elements.reason: The authors describe the search limit (publication year 2015-2019) and provide a justification for it.
There is no evidence that published search approaches or filters were used or cited.
No natural-language processing or text-analysis tools were reported.
No tools used to translate search strings between sources were reported.

elements.quote: The search strategy was pilot tested on a subset of records from the PubMed database.
elements.reason: The authors describe the validation process for the search strategy via pilot testing.
There is no mention of peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS).

elements.quote: To determine our research question's eligibility for a systematic review project, we applied the PEO (Population, Exposure, and Outcomes) nomenclature for systematic reviews 24 , as illustrated in Table 1.
elements.reason: The authors describe the conceptual structure (PEO framework) used to develop the search strategy.

elements.quote: Two skilled reviewers independently screened all the abstracts of the retrieved articles against the eligibility criteria (Table 2)... Full-text articles were retrieved where studies met the inclusion criteria or where there was ambiguity to be screened in greater depth... Two independent reviewers utilised a standardised and pilot tested full-text screening checklist tool
elements.reason: The text explicitly states that two reviewers screened abstracts and two independent reviewers screened full-text articles.

elements.quote: Two skilled reviewers independently screened all the abstracts of the retrieved articles... Two independent reviewers utilised a standardised and pilot tested full-text screening checklist tool
elements.reason: The text confirms that reviewers worked independently at both the abstract and full-text screening stages.

elements.quote: Differences between reviewers at this stage were settled through reaching a consensus among reviewers... At this stage, the disagreement was assessed using Cohen's Kappa coefficient (κ) statistic on Stata 13.0SE... Detected differences between reviewers were resolved through discussion and a third arbitrator.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process for resolving disagreements at both the abstract (consensus) and full-text (discussion and third arbitrator) screening stages.

elements.quote: For more detail, missing details or inconsistencies, the authors of the included studies were contacted by e-mail, if any, with up to three attempts.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process for contacting study investigators to obtain missing details or confirm eligibility.

The manuscript does not mention the need for translation of abstracts or full articles; it states that studies were included in any publication language, implying no translation was required or performed.
The manuscript does not report the use of automation tools (e.g., machine learning screening tools) in the selection process.
No externally derived classifiers were used.
No internally derived classifiers were used.
No machine-learning prioritization tools or screening stopping rules were used.
No crowdsourcing platforms were used.
No previously screened datasets were used to eliminate records.

elements.quote: The data extraction procedure required two professional reviewers who extracted data separately and in duplicate
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that two reviewers were involved in the data extraction process.

elements.quote: The data extraction procedure required two professional reviewers who extracted data separately and in duplicate
elements.reason: The manuscript confirms that the two reviewers worked independently (separately) and in duplicate.

elements.quote: The coordinator resolved disagreements between the two reviewers, and the decision was either taken to have a third reviewer to re-examine the study or extract all the necessary data from the studies concerned, guided by the same extraction process as outlined above.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process for resolving disagreements between data collectors.

elements.quote: For more detail, missing details or inconsistencies, the authors of the included studies were contacted by e-mail, if any, with up to three attempts.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process for contacting study investigators to obtain or confirm data.
No automation tools were used for data collection; the manuscript describes using a Google Form, which is a data entry tool, not an automation tool.
The manuscript does not report using translation methods, and there is no evidence that translation was required.
The manuscript does not describe extracting data from figures using software.
The manuscript does not describe decision rules for selecting data from multiple reports of the same study.

elements.quote: Outcomes of interest are: 1. Obesity 2. Dyslipidaemia 3. Hypertension 4. Underweight 5. Overweight 6. Others (as reported per study)
elements.reason: The review lists the outcomes of interest in Table 1 and further defines them as primary and secondary outcomes in the Methodology section (Step 7a and 7b).

elements.quote: The included studies were cross-sectional study designs, the data for the relationship between food insecurity and key metabolic risk factors were measured and analysed cross-sectionally rather than longitudinally
elements.reason: The review specifies the time frame of measurement for the outcomes as cross-sectional.

elements.quote: In this meta-analysis, we extracted and used measures of associations that were the most adjusted for one or more sets of potential confounders such as socio-demographic and lifestyle factors only to reduce confounding and measurement errors, ensure consistency across studies and reduce bias.
elements.reason: The text specifies that the authors selected specific results (the most adjusted ones) rather than all compatible results, thereby addressing the requirement to specify the scope of data sought.

elements.quote: In this meta-analysis, we extracted and used measures of associations that were the most adjusted for one or more sets of potential confounders such as socio-demographic and lifestyle factors only to reduce confounding and measurement errors, ensure consistency across studies and reduce bias.
elements.reason: The review describes the process used to select results (choosing the most adjusted measures) to reduce bias and ensure consistency.
There is no evidence of changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or importance.
There is no evidence of changes to processes for selecting results.

elements.quote: The primary outcome of interest in the current systematic review was evidence of associations between food insecurity and key metabolic risk factors for diet-sensitive NCDs... Secondly, after identifying the spectrum of key metabolic risk factors associated with food insecurity, we sought to assess the prevalence of these metabolic risk factors among the food-insecure patients
elements.reason: The review explicitly prioritizes the outcomes by designating them as primary and secondary outcomes.

elements.quote: For every study that met our eligibility criteria for inclusion, two reviewers working independently and in duplicate extracted essential data related to study characteristics, assessment of food insecurity, metabolic risk diagnoses, crude prevalence estimates (number of cases divided by the sample size) and outcome of interest measures (effect size data including the prevalence of key metabolic risk factors, measures of prospective associations with 95% confidence intervals, and covariates evaluated).
elements.reason: The authors explicitly list the data items sought for extraction, including study characteristics, food insecurity assessment, metabolic risk diagnoses, prevalence estimates, outcome measures, and covariates.

elements.quote: For more detail, missing details or inconsistencies, the authors of the included studies were contacted by e-mail, if any, with up to three attempts. The studies concerned were excluded after three unsuccessful attempts to contact the author.
elements.reason: The authors describe the procedure for handling missing or unclear information, which involved contacting the original study authors up to three times, with exclusion as the consequence of failure to respond.

elements.quote: A standardised data extraction tool prepared in a Google Form format, based on a checklist provided in the Cochrane Handbook for Systemic Reviews for Intervention , was ­ used 28 .
elements.reason: The authors cite the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions as the tool used to guide the development of their data extraction checklist.

elements.quote: Lastly, to assess study methodological quality (or risk of bias) of all included studies, we used the adopted Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT)-Version ­ 2018 21
elements.reason: The authors specify the tool used (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool) and the version (2018).

elements.quote: The appraisal tool consists of two core assessment domains addressing the external validity (risk of selection, data collection and non-response bias) and five further assessment domains addressing the internal validity (systematic error-the risk of measurement bias and bias related to data analysis) deemed relevant to appraise the methodological quality of cross-sectional ­ studies 22,23 .
elements.reason: The authors describe the domains assessed by the MMAT tool.

elements.quote: In order to generate an overall risk of bias assessment, an overall percentage quality score was calculated for each included study (study quality of reporting) based on the assessment of each domain and the overall risk of bias across domains. The scores were interpreted as of low quality if ≤ 50%-average quality if 51-75%-and high quality if 76-100%.
elements.reason: The authors report the rules used to derive an overall quality/risk of bias judgment (percentage scores and interpretation thresholds).
The authors used an existing tool (MMAT) and did not report adapting it.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool was used.

elements.quote: The methodological quality (or risk of bias) of each included study was assessed by two reviewers independently, using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) - Version ­ 2018 21 . ... Differences in rating quality scores were resolved by discussion among the authors until consensus was reached.
elements.reason: The authors report that two reviewers assessed risk of bias independently and describe the disagreement-resolution procedure.
The authors did not report contacting study investigators to confirm risk-of-bias information.
No automation tools were used for the risk-of-bias assessment.

elements.quote: The prevalence estimates of key metabolic risk factors associated with food insecurity among the food-insecure patients were calculated by meta-analysis. The meta-analysis was performed using the statistical software MetaXL version 5.3... The pooled prevalence of metabolic risk factors and it's 95% confidence interval (CI) were analysed using the random-effects model, utilising the inverse variance method of the DerSimonian-Laird approach
elements.reason: The authors specify that the effect measure used for the meta-analysis of prevalence estimates was the pooled prevalence with 95% confidence intervals. For the primary outcome (associations), they describe a narrative synthesis and report odds ratios (OR) or adjusted odds ratios (AOR) in the results tables (Table 3).
The study did not use specific thresholds to interpret effect sizes (e.g., interpreting an OR of 2.0 as 'large'); it relied on statistical significance (p-values) and confidence intervals.
The manuscript does not describe re-expressing synthesized results using another effect measure.

The choice of effect measure (prevalence for secondary outcomes, odds ratios for primary associations) is standard for the types of data extracted and does not require specific justification beyond standard practice.

elements.quote: Full-article screening yielded 22, which were selected for inclusion in data extraction and were included in the narrative synthesis after passing the methodological quality assessment. Nineteen articles were deemed to be sufficiently homogenous for inclusion in the meta-analysis. ... However, due to the low number of studies that reported stunting, acute respiratory infection (ARI), and left ventricular mass (LVM) types of metabolic risk factors (less than 3), a meta-analysis could not be undertaken for those studies.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process for determining eligibility for synthesis by stating that 22 studies were included in the narrative synthesis, while 19 were included in the meta-analysis based on sufficient homogeneity. It further explains that meta-analyses were not conducted for specific outcomes (stunting, ARI, LVM) because fewer than three studies were available.

elements.quote: In this meta-analysis, we extracted and used measures of associations that were the most adjusted for one or more sets of potential confounders such as socio-demographic and lifestyle factors only to reduce confounding and measurement errors, ensure consistency across studies and reduce bias. For more detail, missing details or inconsistencies, the authors of the included studies were contacted by e-mail, if any, with up to three attempts. The studies concerned were excluded after three unsuccessful attempts to contact the author.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the methods used to handle missing data (contacting authors, then excluding studies) and the approach to data consistency (using the most adjusted measures).

elements.quote: Table 3 presents the baseline characteristics, and significant findings of all the included 22 studies with a total sample of 26,609 (46.8% males) food-insecure participants, with 11,545 (42.1% males) reported prevalence of metabolic risk factors (Table 4).
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the content of the tables used to display results, specifically noting that Table 3 presents baseline characteristics and significant findings, and Table 4 shows pooled prevalence data.

elements.quote: Forest plots were drawn showing the variation of the prevalence among all included studies together with the pooled prevalence estimates.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the graphical methods used, including forest plots for meta-analysis results and a map (Figure 2) to show geographic distribution.

elements.quote: The included studies were manually coded into strata' as explained above, and presented in the compiled summary of the extracted data table (see Table 3).
elements.reason: The manuscript explains the basis for grouping studies in tables and figures, specifically using strata (Adverse, Non-significant, Inconclusive) and gender.
The manuscript does not utilize non-standard graphs; therefore, a rationale is not required.

elements.quote: The meta-analysis was performed using the statistical software MetaXL version 5.3 (EpiGear International, Sunrise Beach, Queenland, Australia) to combine all studies' prevalence 31.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the software (MetaXL) and version number (5.3) used for the meta-analysis.

elements.quote: Furthermore, the reporting of the association effects relative to food insecurity was inconsistent across included studies (illustrated in Table 3); thus a narrative synthesis was performed to identify the specific key metabolic risk factors associated with food insecurity in sub-Saharan Africa.
elements.reason: The authors describe and justify the use of narrative synthesis for the primary outcome (associations between food insecurity and metabolic risk factors) due to inconsistency in reporting across studies.

elements.quote: The pooled prevalence of metabolic risk factors and it's 95% confidence interval (CI) were analysed using the random-effects model, utilising the inverse variance method of the DerSimonian-Laird approach to estimate the heterogeneity between-study population 31.
elements.reason: The authors report the use of a random-effects model for the meta-analysis.

elements.quote: The pooled prevalence of metabolic risk factors and it's 95% confidence interval (CI) were analysed using the random-effects model, utilising the inverse variance method of the DerSimonian-Laird approach to estimate the heterogeneity between-study population 31.
elements.reason: The authors report the use of the inverse variance method for the meta-analysis.

elements.quote: Therefore, all meta-analyses were statistically, appraised for significant inter-study heterogeneity by using the I 2 statistics for statistical significance of heterogeneity (i.e., the percentage of variance not due to studies-wide sampling error), where the significance was considered as per the guidelines of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions 28 . Consequently, an I 2 value of ≥ 75% suggests a substantial heterogeneity.
elements.reason: The authors describe the use of the I-squared statistic to identify and quantify statistical heterogeneity.

elements.quote: The pooled prevalence of metabolic risk factors and it's 95% confidence interval (CI) were analysed using the random-effects model, utilising the inverse variance method of the DerSimonian-Laird approach to estimate the heterogeneity between-study population 31.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state the use of the DerSimonian-Laird approach as the between-study variance estimator for the random-effects meta-analysis.
The manuscript does not explicitly state the method used to calculate confidence intervals for the summary effect (e.g., Wald-type, Clopper-Pearson, etc.), although it mentions reporting 95% CIs.
No other specific random-effects implementation details (beyond model, variance estimator, and software) were required or reported.
The meta-analysis was not Bayesian; it used the DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model.
The manuscript does not describe methods used to account for statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study (e.g., if multiple outcomes were extracted from one study).

elements.quote: However, due to the low number of studies that reported stunting, acute respiratory infection (ARI), and left ventricular mass (LVM) types of metabolic risk factors (less than 3), a meta-analysis could not be undertaken for those studies.
elements.reason: The authors identify planned syntheses (meta-analysis for specific outcomes) that were judged inappropriate due to the small number of studies and provide the reason.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the influence of the difference in age, gender, publication year, and geographic area among the included studies.

elements.quote: Comparison with previous studies. Previous systematic reviews and several cross-sectional studies have contributed to the evidence that food insecurity is associated with metabolic risk factors on the causal pathway to diet-sensitive NCDs. In the current review, the results of both analyses show imperative similarities, consistent with and expands the results of earlier reports. In addition, the current review yields new evidence visualising variation patterns in the prevalence of specific key metabolic risk factors by gender and geographic area among the food insecure population in sub-Saharan Africa. ... Similar to our systematic review, Arenas et al. 5 found an adverse association between exposure to food insecurity and dyslipidemia, as reported from 7 peer-reviewed manuscripts published between 2006 and 2015, involving only US participants. ... A recent review by Beltran et al. 57 showed that most studies in the USA that indicate a correlation between food insecurity and hypertension correspond to self-reporting of conditions. ... On the other hand, Arenas et al. 5 found no consistent literature-wide association between body mass index and food insecurity-status; only 18 studies out of 37 reported a statistically significant association, which is more studies than we report in our current systematic review.
